items.stem: Where are chromosomes found in a cell?
items.answer: In the nucleus
items.markingKey: Chromosomes are long DNA molecules inside the nucleus.

items.stem: Explain why chromosomes in body cells are found in pairs.
items.answer: One chromosome of each pair comes from the mother (egg) and one from the father (sperm).
items.markingKey: one from each parent [1]; via egg and sperm [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why identical twins have the same genes.
items.answer: They develop from one fertilised egg that splits into two, so both have the same DNA.
items.markingKey: one fertilised egg splits [1]; same DNA [1] [2]

items.stem: A body cell of a dog has 78 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in its sperm or egg cells and in a fertilised egg.
items.answer: 39 in a gamete; 78 in a fertilised egg

items.stem: A body cell of a cow has 60 chromosomes. (a) State the number of pairs of chromosomes. (b) State the number in a gamete. (c) Explain why gametes must have half the number of chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) 30 pairs (b) 30 (c) At fertilisation two gametes fuse, so the fertilised egg gets the full number (60) and the number stays the same each generation.
items.markingKey: (a) 30 [1] (b) 30 [1] (c) fusion restores full number [1] [3]

items.stem: A biology class in Bogotá looks at cells from a garden pea under a microscope. Each body cell contains 14 chromosomes. (a) Explain what a gene does. (b) Describe the contribution of Rosalind Franklin to the discovery of the structure of DNA.
items.answer: (a) It is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for a characteristic (by coding for a protein). (b) She produced X-ray images of DNA (Photo 51) showing it was a helix; Watson and Crick used this to build their model.
items.markingKey: (a) section of DNA [1]; instructions for a characteristic [1] [2] (b) X-ray images [1]; used by Watson and Crick [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why mature human red blood cells cannot pass on genetic information.
items.answer: They have no nucleus, so they contain no chromosomes or DNA.
items.markingKey: no nucleus [1]; no DNA [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how Watson and Crick used the work of other scientists.
items.answer: They used Franklin and Wilkins’ X-ray images and other chemical data to build their model; science builds on shared evidence.
items.markingKey: used X-ray evidence [1]; collaboration / building on others [1] [2]

items.stem: A body cell of a rice plant has 24 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in its sperm or egg cells and in a fertilised egg.
items.answer: 12 in a gamete; 24 in a fertilised egg

items.stem: A biology class in Doha looks at cells from an onion under a microscope. Each body cell contains 16 chromosomes. (a) State where the chromosomes are found in the cell. (b) Explain why offspring are similar to, but not identical to, either parent.
items.answer: (a) In the nucleus. (b) They receive half their chromosomes (genes) from each parent, giving a new combination.
items.markingKey: (a) In the nucleus [1] (b) half from each parent [1]; new combination [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas reads that the body cells of a mouse each contain 40 chromosomes, and human body cells contain 46. (a) State where the chromosomes are found in the cell. (b) Describe the structure of a chromosome. (c) Explain why offspring are similar to, but not identical to, either parent.
items.answer: (a) In the nucleus. (b) A long, coiled molecule of DNA (a double helix) carrying many genes along its length. (c) They receive half their chromosomes (genes) from each parent, giving a new combination.
items.markingKey: (a) In the nucleus [1] (b) long DNA molecule [1]; carries many genes [1] [2] (c) half from each parent [1]; new combination [1] [2]

items.stem: Which pair of sex chromosomes does a human female have?
items.answer: XX
items.markingKey: Females XX, males XY.

items.stem: Explain why approximately equal numbers of boys and girls are born.
items.answer: Half of the sperm carry X and half carry Y, and each has an equal chance of fertilising the egg, so XX and XY are equally likely.
items.markingKey: half sperm X, half Y [1]; equal chance of fertilising [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why brothers and sisters with the same parents are not identical.
items.answer: Each gamete carries a different combination of the parents’ chromosomes, so each child inherits a different mix.
items.markingKey: gametes differ [1]; different combinations inherited [1] [2]

items.stem: A hospital in Santiago expects 1000 births this year. Estimate how many babies will be boys and explain your answer.
items.answer: About 500
items.markingKey: 1000 × 0.5 = 500 [1]; half of sperm carry Y / chance 0.5 [1] [2]

items.stem: A couple plan to have 3 children. (a) Draw or describe a genetic diagram to show the chance of each child being a girl. (b) Calculate the probability that all 3 children are girls.
items.answer: (a) XX × XY → gametes X and X, Y → offspring XX : XY = 1 : 1, so 0.5 girl each time (b) 0.5^3 = 0.125 (1 in 8)

items.stem: A couple plan to have 4 children. (a) Draw or describe a genetic diagram to show the chance of each child being a girl. (b) Calculate the probability that all 4 children are girls. (c) Explain why the probability for the next child is unchanged even after several girls.
items.answer: (a) XX × XY → gametes X and X, Y → offspring XX : XY = 1 : 1, so 0.5 girl each time (b) 0.5^4 = 0.0625 (1 in 16) (c) Each fertilisation is a separate event; the chance of an X or Y sperm is always 0.5.
items.markingKey: (a) gametes [1]; 1 : 1 ratio [1] (b) 0.5^4 = 0.0625 [1] (c) independent events [1] [4]

items.stem: Records at a hospital in Muscat show 2000 births in one year: 1020 boys and 980 girls. (a) Suggest why the numbers are not exactly 50% boys and 50% girls. (b) Describe what happens at fertilisation.
items.answer: (a) Fertilisation is random (chance), so small differences from the expected ratio occur, especially in small samples. (b) The nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an egg, giving a fertilised egg with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
items.markingKey: (a) chance / random [1]; sample size [1] [2] (b) nuclei fuse [1]; 46 / 23 pairs [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya studies birth records for a town: of 3000 babies born, 1460 were boys. (a) Calculate the percentage of babies that were boys. (b) Explain, using a genetic diagram, why about half of babies are boys.
items.answer: (a) 48.7% (b) Mother XX makes eggs all X; father XY makes sperm X or Y in equal numbers; fertilisation gives XX : XY = 1 : 1.

items.stem: Which sex chromosomes can a human sperm cell carry?
items.answer: Either X or Y
items.markingKey: Half of sperm carry X, half carry Y.

items.stem: Which sex chromosome does every human egg cell carry?
items.answer: X
items.markingKey: Females are XX, so every egg carries an X.

items.stem: Explain why a child has some features of the mother and some of the father.
items.answer: Half of the chromosomes (genes) come from the mother’s egg and half from the father’s sperm.
items.markingKey: half from each parent [1]; genes control features [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara says: "The mother decides whether the baby is a boy or a girl because the baby grows inside her." Explain why Zara is wrong.
items.answer: Every egg carries X; the sperm carries X or Y, so the father’s sperm determines the sex.
items.markingKey: egg always X [1]; sperm X or Y determines sex [1] [2]

items.stem: A hospital in Hanoi expects 2400 births this year. Estimate how many babies will be boys and explain your answer.
items.answer: About 1200
items.markingKey: 2400 × 0.5 = 1200 [1]; half of sperm carry Y / chance 0.5 [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas studies birth records for a town: of 1500 babies born, 798 were boys. (a) Suggest why the numbers are not exactly 50% boys and 50% girls. (b) State the number of chromosomes in a human sperm cell and the sex chromosome(s) it may carry.
items.answer: (a) Fertilisation is random (chance), so small differences from the expected ratio occur, especially in small samples. (b) 23; either X or Y.
items.markingKey: (a) chance / random [1]; sample size [1] [2] (b) 23 [1]; X or Y [1] [2]

items.stem: Records at a hospital in Dhaka show 1500 births in one year: 770 boys and 730 girls. (a) Calculate the percentage of babies that were boys. (b) Suggest why the numbers are not exactly 50% boys and 50% girls. (c) State the number of chromosomes in a human sperm cell and the sex chromosome(s) it may carry.
items.answer: (a) 51.3% (b) Fertilisation is random (chance), so small differences from the expected ratio occur, especially in small samples. (c) 23; either X or Y.

items.stem: Which is an example of continuous variation?
items.answer: Height
items.markingKey: Height can take any value within a range.

items.stem: Explain why height is affected by both genes and the environment.
items.answer: Genes set the possible range of height; diet, health and exercise affect how tall a person actually grows.
items.markingKey: genes set potential [1]; environment (diet etc.) affects outcome [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why studies of identical twins are useful for finding the causes of variation.
items.answer: Identical twins have the same genes, so any differences between them must be caused by the environment.
items.markingKey: same genes [1]; differences due to environment [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas measures the leaf length of 8 leaves from one tree (mm): 46, 76, 78, 52, 51, 49, 62, 62. Calculate the range and the mean.
items.answer: range 32 mm; mean 59.5 mm

items.stem: Elena measures the foot length of 10 students in a class (cm): 21, 21, 27, 24, 26, 26, 21, 21, 27, 25. (a) Calculate the mean. (b) State the type of variation and the type of graph you would use to display a larger set of these data. (c) Suggest one environmental factor that could affect this characteristic.
items.answer: (a) 23.9 cm (b) Continuous; histogram (c) Diet during growth.
items.markingKey: (a) 23.9 [1] (b) continuous and histogram [1] (c) valid factor [1] [3]

items.stem: Kenji grows 12 seedlings from the same parent plant in bright light and 12 in shade. After four weeks the mean leaf length is 58 mm in bright light and 76 mm in the shade. (a) Explain whether this variation is caused by genes or by the environment. (b) Explain why a mean of many plants is used.
items.answer: (a) The environment, because the plants have the same genes (same parent / cuttings); only the light differs. (b) Individual plants vary; a mean reduces the effect of unusual plants and is more reliable.
items.markingKey: (a) environment [1]; same genes so difference due to light [1] [2] (b) natural variation [1]; more reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a bar chart is used for blood group data but a histogram is used for heights.
items.answer: Blood groups are separate categories (discontinuous); heights are continuous data that must be grouped into touching classes.
items.markingKey: blood group categories [1]; height continuous / grouped [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why plants of the same variety grown in the shade are often taller but paler than those in sunlight.
items.answer: The environment (light) affects growth: shaded plants grow taller to reach light and make less chlorophyll; their genes are the same.
items.markingKey: environmental cause [1]; light affects growth / colour [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel measures the hand span of 9 students in a class (cm): 18, 16, 17, 21, 17, 21, 19, 16, 20. Calculate the range and the mean.
items.answer: range 5 cm; mean 18.3 cm

items.stem: In a school garden in Istanbul, 15 cuttings from one plant (so with identical genes) are planted in shade and 15 in full sun. The mean leaf length is 60 mm in shade and 50 mm in sun. (a) State the type of variation shown by leaf length and give a reason. (b) Suggest why the plants in the shade grow larger leaves. (c) Explain why a mean of many plants is used.
items.answer: (a) Continuous, because leaf length can take any value within a range. (b) Larger leaves have a bigger surface area to absorb the limited light for photosynthesis. (c) Individual plants vary; a mean reduces the effect of unusual plants and is more reliable.
items.markingKey: (a) continuous [1]; any value in range [1] [2] (b) larger surface area [1]; absorb more light [1] [2] (c) natural variation [1]; more reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
items.answer: Charles Darwin
items.markingKey: Darwin (with Alfred Russel Wallace) published in 1858–1859.

items.stem: Explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria become common.
items.answer: A few bacteria have a mutation giving resistance; the antibiotic kills the others; the resistant ones survive, reproduce and pass on the resistance gene.
items.markingKey: variation / mutation [1]; non-resistant killed [1]; resistant survive and reproduce [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why giraffes have long necks, according to natural selection.
items.answer: Giraffes varied in neck length; those with longer necks reached more food, survived and bred more, passing on genes for long necks over many generations.
items.markingKey: variation [1]; survival and breeding of longer-necked [1]; genes passed on over generations [1] [3]

items.stem: Scientists released 400 pale and 600 dark peppered moths in a clean wood with pale, lichen-covered tree trunks. Later they recaptured 56 pale and 36 dark moths. Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured.
items.answer: pale 14%; dark 6%

items.stem: Scientists released 400 pale and 300 dark peppered moths in a clean wood with pale, lichen-covered tree trunks. Later they recaptured 64 pale and 18 dark moths. (a) Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured. (b) Explain why percentages are compared rather than numbers. (c) Explain the results in terms of natural selection.
items.answer: (a) pale 16%, dark 6% (b) Different numbers of each type were released. (c) Pale moths were better camouflaged on these trunks, so birds ate fewer of them; more survived to breed and pass on their genes.
items.markingKey: (a) both percentages [1] (b) different numbers released [1] (c) camouflage → fewer eaten [1] [3]

items.stem: Scientists released 500 pale and 600 dark peppered moths in a clean wood with pale, lichen-covered tree trunks. Later they recaptured 70 pale and 36 dark moths. (a) Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured. (b) Explain why percentages are compared rather than numbers. (c) Explain the results in terms of natural selection.
items.answer: (a) pale 14%, dark 6% (b) Different numbers of each type were released. (c) Pale moths were better camouflaged on these trunks, so birds ate fewer of them; more survived to breed and pass on their genes.
items.markingKey: (a) both percentages [1] (b) different numbers released [1] (c) camouflage → fewer eaten [1]; survive, breed, pass on genes [1] [4]

items.stem: On a Galápagos island, the mean beak depth of a population of finches was 9.8 mm. After a severe drought, when only large, hard seeds were left, the mean beak depth of the survivors’ offspring was 10.2 mm. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth. (b) Predict what might happen to beak depth if several wet years produce plenty of small seeds.
items.answer: (a) 4.08% (b) Mean beak depth may decrease again, as smaller-beaked birds feed efficiently and survive well.

items.stem: Scientists studying ground finches recorded a mean beak depth of 9.6 mm before a drought. The drought killed most plants with small seeds. In the next generation the mean beak depth was 10.0 mm. (a) Explain how natural selection caused this change. (b) Explain why the change can only happen if beak depth is at least partly controlled by genes.
items.answer: (a) Beak depth varied; birds with deeper beaks could crack the large hard seeds, so they survived and bred; they passed on genes for deep beaks, so the mean increased. (b) Only genetic characteristics are passed to offspring; features caused only by the environment are not inherited.
items.markingKey: (a) variation [1]; deep-beaked birds survive [1]; breed and pass on genes [1] [3] (b) genes inherited [1]; environmental features not passed on [1] [2]

items.stem: In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to survive?
options: Those best adapted to their environment
items.answer: Those best adapted to their environment
items.markingKey: Better-adapted individuals survive, breed and pass on their genes.

items.stem: What do surviving individuals pass on to their offspring?
options: Characteristics they gained during life, such as strong muscles from exercise
Their genes, including those for the useful characteristic
items.answer: Their genes, including those for the useful characteristic
items.markingKey: Offspring inherit the advantageous genes.

items.stem: Explain why patients are told to finish a course of antibiotics.
items.answer: To kill all the bacteria, including the slightly more resistant ones, so resistant bacteria do not survive and multiply.
items.markingKey: kill all bacteria [1]; prevent resistant survivors [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists released 200 pale and 600 dark peppered moths in a polluted wood with soot-darkened tree trunks. Later they recaptured 28 pale and 150 dark moths. Which moths survived better?
items.answer: dark moths
items.markingKey: Recapture: pale 14%, dark 25%.

items.stem: A patient has an infection of 1.0 × 10⁷ bacteria. 2% of them carry a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills all the bacteria that are not resistant. Calculate the number of bacteria that survive.

A patient has an infection of 2.0 × 10⁶ bacteria. 1% of them carry a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills all the bacteria that are not resistant. (a) Calculate the number that survive. (b) The survivors double in number every 20 minutes. Calculate the number after 120 minutes. (c) Explain why the antibiotic will no longer cure the infection.
items.answer: (a) 2.0 × 10⁴ (b) 2.0 × 10⁴ × 2^6 = 1.3 × 10⁶ (c) All the new bacteria have inherited the resistance gene, so the antibiotic cannot kill them.
items.markingKey: (a) 2.0 × 10⁴ [1] (b) 6 doublings → 1.3 × 10⁶ [1] (c) all resistant / inherited [1] [3]

items.stem: What are chromosomes made of?
items.answer: DNA
items.markingKey: Each chromosome is a very long DNA molecule (with proteins).

items.stem: Explain why a gene can affect a characteristic such as eye colour.
items.answer: The gene carries the instructions for making a protein (e.g. pigment), which produces the characteristic.
items.markingKey: instructions for a protein [1]; protein gives characteristic [1] [2]

items.stem: A body cell of a garden pea has 14 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in its sperm or egg cells and in a fertilised egg.
items.answer: 7 in a gamete; 14 in a fertilised egg

items.stem: A biology class in Lisbon looks at cells from a maize (corn) under a microscope. Each body cell contains 20 chromosomes. (a) State where the chromosomes are found in the cell. (b) State how many chromosomes are in a maize (corn) sperm or egg cell. (c) Describe the contribution of Rosalind Franklin to the discovery of the structure of DNA.
items.answer: (a) In the nucleus. (b) 10 (c) She produced X-ray images of DNA (Photo 51) showing it was a helix; Watson and Crick used this to build their model.
items.markingKey: (a) In the nucleus [1] (b) 10: 10 [1] (c) X-ray images [1]; used by Watson and Crick [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the probability that a baby will be a boy?
items.markingKey: Half of sperm carry Y.

items.stem: Describe how to show sex determination using a genetic diagram.
items.answer: Write the parents as XX and XY, their gametes as X (egg) and X or Y (sperm), and combine them in a grid to give XX and XY in a 1 : 1 ratio.
items.markingKey: parents and gametes shown [1]; offspring 1 : 1 [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace claims: "The mother decides whether the baby is a boy or a girl because the baby grows inside her." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Every egg carries X; the sperm carries X or Y, so the father’s sperm determines the sex.
items.markingKey: egg always X [1]; sperm X or Y determines sex [1] [2]

items.stem: A hospital in Bangkok expects 1000 births this year. Estimate how many babies will be boys and explain your answer.
items.answer: About 500

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Identical twins grow up in different countries and have different masses. This is caused by … (b) Which is an example of continuous variation?
items.answer: (a) the environment (b) Height
items.markingKey: (a) They have identical genes, so differences come from diet, exercise, etc. (b) Height can take any value within a range.

items.stem: Explain why variation within a species is important.
items.answer: Some individuals may be better suited to changes in the environment and survive, so the species is less likely to die out.
items.markingKey: some individuals better adapted [1]; species survives change [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara measures the leaf length of 8 leaves from one tree (mm): 67, 72, 62, 60, 60, 75, 42, 46. Calculate the range and the mean.
items.answer: range 33 mm; mean 60.5 mm

items.stem: Explain why fossils provide evidence for evolution.
items.answer: Fossils in rocks of different ages show that organisms have changed gradually over time.
items.markingKey: fossils in different rock ages [1]; show gradual change [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why natural selection is slow in large animals but fast in bacteria.
items.answer: Bacteria reproduce in minutes, so many generations pass quickly; large animals take years per generation.
items.markingKey: generation time [1]; bacteria very short [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara measures the foot length of 9 students in a class (cm): 24, 24, 22, 21, 21, 21, 24, 21, 27. Calculate the range and the mean.
items.answer: range 6 cm; mean 22.8 cm

items.stem: Kenji grows 15 seedlings from the same parent plant in bright light and 15 in shade. After four weeks the mean leaf length is 54 mm in bright light and 72 mm in the shade. (a) State the type of variation shown by leaf length and give a reason. (b) Explain why a mean of many plants is used.
items.answer: (a) Continuous, because leaf length can take any value within a range. (b) Individual plants vary; a mean reduces the effect of unusual plants and is more reliable.
items.markingKey: (a) continuous [1]; any value in range [1] [2] (b) natural variation [1]; more reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria become common. (b) Explain why patients are told to finish a course of antibiotics.
items.answer: (a) A few bacteria have a mutation giving resistance; the antibiotic kills the others; the resistant ones survive, reproduce and pass on the resistance gene. (b) To kill all the bacteria, including the slightly more resistant ones, so resistant bacteria do not survive and multiply.
items.markingKey: (a) variation / mutation [1]; non-resistant killed [1]; resistant survive and reproduce [1] [3] (b) kill all bacteria [1]; prevent resistant survivors [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho says: "Giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves, and their babies were born with longer necks." Explain why Sipho is wrong.
items.answer: Characteristics acquired during life are not inherited; giraffes with genes for longer necks survived and passed those genes on.
items.markingKey: acquired features not inherited [1]; selection of genetic variation [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists released 300 pale and 400 dark peppered moths in a clean wood with pale, lichen-covered tree trunks. Later they recaptured 48 pale and 20 dark moths. Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured.
items.answer: pale 16%; dark 5%

items.stem: A patient has an infection of 2.0 × 10⁶ bacteria. 1% of them carry a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills all the bacteria that are not resistant. Calculate the number of bacteria that survive.

A patient has an infection of 1.0 × 10⁷ bacteria. 10% of them carry a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills all the bacteria that are not resistant. (a) Calculate the number that survive. (b) The survivors double in number every 20 minutes. Calculate the number after 100 minutes. (c) Explain why the antibiotic will no longer cure the infection.
items.answer: (a) 1.0 × 10⁶ (b) 1.0 × 10⁶ × 2^5 = 3.2 × 10⁷ (c) All the new bacteria have inherited the resistance gene, so the antibiotic cannot kill them.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.0 × 10⁶ [1] (b) 5 doublings → 3.2 × 10⁷ [1] (c) all resistant / inherited [1] [3]

items.stem: Scientists studying ground finches recorded a mean beak depth of 9.4 mm before a drought. The drought killed most plants with small seeds. In the next generation the mean beak depth was 10.0 mm. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth. (b) Explain why the change can only happen if beak depth is at least partly controlled by genes. (c) Predict what might happen to beak depth if several wet years produce plenty of small seeds.
items.answer: (a) 6.38% (b) Only genetic characteristics are passed to offspring; features caused only by the environment are not inherited. (c) Mean beak depth may decrease again, as smaller-beaked birds feed efficiently and survive well.
items.markingKey: (a) (10.0 − 9.4) ÷ 9.4 × 100 [1] = 6.38% [1] [2] (b) genes inherited [1]; environmental features not passed on [1] [2] (c) decrease [1]; reason [1] [2]
